document_title: Texas A&M says Florida's state drone team made its CLARKE disaster damage reader standard procedure
_note: Caption carried verbatim from caption.txt. Slide strings polished from storyboard.md and held to the claim quotes in claims.json. Every numeral is in claims.json or figures.json. Drawn to illustrate appears only on S1, S4 and S7. S9's absence is scoped to the November 24th release and the project site, as the fact check recorded it.
caption:
Texas A&M says Florida's state drone team made its tool standard procedure.

CLARKE rates the damage to each building in a color coded view. A road model flags damaged roads so crews can route around them. A trained operator reviews every assessment before it reaches decision makers.

Tom Manzini of the development team says CLARKE turns drone imagery into damage assessments in minutes instead of 18 to 24 hours.

Texas A&M says the models learned from more than 21,000 damaged homes in 10 major disasters, Hurricane Harvey among them. It says 125 responders from 63 agencies in 14 states and Puerto Rico have trained on CLARKE. The November 24th release and the project site name no Texas agency or county among its users.

How many of those 63 agencies are in Texas?

#TexasAM #CLARKE #HurricaneHarvey

S1.headline: Every roof, read in minutes
S1.body: Texas A&M's CLARKE reads drone imagery after a disaster and returns a detailed damage assessment within minutes. Neighborhood and colors drawn to illustrate.
strings: Texas A&M's CLARKE reads drone imagery after a disaster and returns a detailed damage assessment within minutes. Neighborhood and colors drawn to illustrate.

S2.headline: 18 to 24 hours, the old way
S2.body: Tom Manzini of the development team says CLARKE turns drone imagery into damage assessments in minutes instead of 18 to 24 hours. Gathering damage information can take days, particularly in rural areas. Roadside marker posts count off the hours.
strings: Tom Manzini of the development team says CLARKE turns drone imagery into damage assessments in minutes instead of 18 to 24 hours. Gathering damage information can take days, particularly in rural areas. Roadside marker posts count off the hours.

S3.headline: Many pictures, one map
S3.body: The drone images are stitched into one georectified orthomosaic and aligned to building and road footprints. Given a finished orthomosaic, the project site says CLARKE assesses roughly 2,000 buildings in about 7 minutes.
strings: The drone images are stitched into one georectified orthomosaic and aligned to building and road footprints. Given a finished orthomosaic, the project site says CLARKE assesses roughly 2,000 buildings in about 7 minutes.

S4.headline: Then every roof is judged
S4.body: The Building Damage Assessment rates the damage to each individual building and gives responders a color coded view, structure by structure. Colors drawn to illustrate.
strings: The Building Damage Assessment rates the damage to each individual building and gives responders a color coded view, structure by structure. Colors drawn to illustrate.

S5.headline: Taught partly on Harvey
S5.body: The models learned from drone imagery of more than 21,000 damaged homes in 10 major disasters, Hurricane Harvey and Hurricane Ian among them. One plate stands for one of the dataset's 265 orthomosaics, drawn to illustrate.
strings: The models learned from drone imagery of more than 21,000 damaged homes in 10 major disasters, Hurricane Harvey and Hurricane Ian among them. One plate stands for one of the dataset's 265 orthomosaics, drawn to illustrate.

S6.headline: A person checks every map
S6.body: A trained operator reviews every assessment before it reaches decision makers. CLARKE's models are designed to run entirely in the field. No wireless transmission of imagery is needed to generate an assessment. Its results come out as GeoJSON and KML map files.
strings: A trained operator reviews every assessment before it reaches decision makers. CLARKE's models are designed to run entirely in the field. No wireless transmission of imagery is needed to generate an assessment. Its results come out as GeoJSON and KML map files.

S7.headline: The road out
S7.body: A road model identifies road damage and obstructions. Crews can then find routes around damaged roads and other obstacles. Filled roofs show assessments after review, drawn to illustrate.
strings: A road model identifies road damage and obstructions. Crews can then find routes around damaged roads and other obstacles. Filled roofs show assessments after review, drawn to illustrate.

S8.headline: 125 responders, 63 agencies
S8.body: Texas A&M says 125 emergency responders from 63 agencies in 14 states and Puerto Rico have trained on CLARKE. One helmet stands for one responder.
strings: Texas A&M says 125 emergency responders from 63 agencies in 14 states and Puerto Rico have trained on CLARKE. One helmet stands for one responder.

S9.headline: Texas A&M says Florida's team uses it
S9.body: Texas A&M says Florida's state drone team now uses CLARKE as standard operating procedure. It was deployed in Florida and Pennsylvania in the 2024 hurricane season. The November 24th release and the project site name no Texas agency or county among its users. Street drawn to illustrate. Watch for the first.
